market: A hard risk-off close on Thursday: IWM (the small-cap ETF) fell 2.18% to 264.22, SPY 1.96%, QQQ 2.19%, and the VIX jumped 15.8% to 28.44. The 10-year yield sits at 5.05% and the reported backdrop is Fed minutes that left a December hike open, which hits small caps hardest because they borrow more and often at floating rates. One lesser-known source ties the afternoon reversal to selling after a large AI listing; that cause is not corroborated, but the index numbers are from our own quotes. Small-cap decliners mostly tracked the tape with no news of their own. Overnight, crude is steady near $82.85 and Yahoo shows gold futures down about 4.3% to roughly $3,528, a large move I could not confirm elsewhere. In this tape I favour names with their own reason to move (fresh insider buying after a reset, held up on a down day) over levered, rate-sensitive ones.

verdicts.name: HMH
verdicts.thesis: The CFO put about $1.65M of his own money into the stock, with the CEO alongside, two weeks after a Q3 miss and guidance cut took it down 38%. Management calls the Middle East shortfall deferral, orders beat revenue (book-to-bill 1.12), and the stock rose 1.4% on a day small caps fell 2.2%. A CFO buy of that size after a reset is the strongest signal on tonight's list and the selling looks spent.
verdicts.dilution: No company share sales, ATM, warrants or convertibles found. Cash $90.1M, net long-term debt $196.7M, nothing due until June 2028, Q3 free cash flow negative $11.6M. The real overhang is a resale registration for up to 31.9M Class A shares held by Baker Hughes and Akastor (supplement dated Nov 4); the company gets no proceeds and no lock-up was found.
verdicts.wrong_if: Baker Hughes or Akastor launches a sale of their registered shares, or the stock closes below the November low near $10.31.

verdicts.name: OFRM
verdicts.thesis: A toddler-bar recall and guidance cut knocked a company growing sales 35% from about $16 to $9; four insiders, including the chief executive, bought this week and the stock rose 8.9% on a day small caps fell 2.2%. It has no debt and $106M of cash against roughly $30M of recall cost, so the damage is bounded and the recovery toward the pre-recall price has buyers behind it. The risk is that the 35% bounce off the low has already paid most of it.
verdicts.dilution: Nothing open found. Cash $106.4M at Sept 30, debt zero after repaying the credit line with February IPO proceeds, convertible notes and preferred warrants gone, no shelf or follow-on seen. Recall cost of about $30M is covered by cash, so a rescue raise looks unlikely.
verdicts.wrong_if: Injury reports, an FDA escalation, a second recall or a retailer dropping the brand; or the stock gives back all of Thursday's gain and closes below $11.30.

verdicts.name: NPCE
verdicts.thesis: The CEO, CFO and a director each bought about $100K in the open market days after a Q3 miss and guidance cut took the stock from $13 to $8. Management blames a few large accounts and a field reorganisation and says Q4 cases have started to recover; margins and costs improved even as growth stalled. Three senior buyers together after a 38% reset, in a stock that barely fell on a bad day, is a fair bounce setup, though it is thin and has no dated catalyst.
